variants.title: Run the experiment path
variants.context: An experiment moves from a product question to a rollout decision in four steps: frame the decision, validate assignment, run to the plan, then decide and preserve the evidence. Analysis cannot repair assignment that was already broken.
variants.prompt: A ranking change is proposed for the main feed. Put the steps in order from product question to rollout decision.

items.text: Run to the plan: collect the required independent units across a representative window without rewriting the success rule.
Validate assignment: run an A/A check, verify deterministic bucketing, record exposure, and investigate sample-ratio mismatch.
Frame the decision: define eligibility, unit, treatment, primary metric, minimum detectable effect, guardrails, and owner.
Decide and preserve: combine effect size, uncertainty, guardrails, and segments, then ship gradually or roll back with a record.

variants.hint: One step exists so nobody reads outcomes from a broken comparison.
variants.explanation: Assignment is validated before outcomes are read, because analysis cannot repair bucketing that changed across sessions.

variants.title: Run the experiment path
variants.context: An experiment moves from a product question to a rollout decision in four steps: frame the decision, validate assignment, run to the plan, then decide and preserve the evidence. Analysis cannot repair assignment that was already broken.
variants.prompt: A pricing model is tested where teammates in the same account see each other's quotes. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Run to the plan: accumulate enough independent accounts, not enough users, before reading the primary metric.
Decide and preserve: report the effect at the account level with its interval and keep the exclusion list with the decision.
Validate assignment: confirm every member of an account lands in one variant and that exposure is logged per account.
Frame the decision: choose the account as the assignment unit because teammates influence one another.

variants.hint: The unit that carries the interference is the unit that carries the statistics.
variants.explanation: When the treatment acts at a broader boundary, the unit, the validity checks, and the effective sample size all move to that boundary.

variants.title: Run the experiment path
variants.context: An experiment moves from a product question to a rollout decision in four steps: frame the decision, validate assignment, run to the plan, then decide and preserve the evidence. Analysis cannot repair assignment that was already broken.
variants.prompt: A test is stopped early because the dashboard showed a large win on day two. Put the steps in order to show what was skipped.

items.text: Validate assignment: exposure logs and sample-ratio checks should have cleared before any outcome was read.
Decide and preserve: only then may effect size, guardrails, and segments produce a rollout action and an evidence record.
Run to the plan: the required independent units and a representative window were still incomplete on day two.
Frame the decision: the stopping rule, minimum runtime, and primary metric were fixed before traffic was sent.

variants.hint: Ask which step the early read jumped over.
variants.explanation: Unplanned peeking spends the error budget the plan assumed, so a designed sequential rule is required when continuous decisions are needed.

variants.title: Trace one unit through the test
variants.context: One traceable experiment path runs from eligibility through a deterministic bucket, an exposure event, the outcome join, and finally the decision record. Assignment establishes intent; the exposure event proves the unit met the treatment.
variants.prompt: A single user passes through a running experiment. Put the stages of that path in order.

items.text: Stable bucket: the experiment ID, assignment unit, and salt hash into a repeatable control or treatment bucket.
Decision record: estimates, intervals, segments, guardrails, exclusions, and the rollout action are preserved.
Outcome join: eligible outcomes attach through the predefined attribution window and deduplication rule.
Eligibility: the frozen population and mutual-exclusion rules admit the unit into the experiment.
Exposure log: the delivered experience is recorded with experiment, variant, unit, timestamp, and treatment version.

variants.hint: Assignment states intent; one later stage proves the experience was actually delivered.
variants.explanation: Randomization only produces comparable groups when bucketing is deterministic and outcomes are joined to observed exposure.

variants.title: Trace one unit through the test
variants.context: One traceable experiment path runs from eligibility through a deterministic bucket, an exposure event, the outcome join, and finally the decision record. Assignment establishes intent; the exposure event proves the unit met the treatment.
variants.prompt: An analyst finds users with outcomes but no exposure row. Put the stages in order to locate where the path broke.

items.text: Stable bucket: confirm the same unit and salt produce one repeatable variant on every request.
Eligibility: confirm the users actually satisfied the frozen population rule for this experiment.
Exposure log: check whether the delivery event fired at all for the variant that is missing rows.
Decision record: hold the estimate until the exclusions and their reason are written down.
Outcome join: check whether the attribution window attached outcomes to units that were never exposed.

variants.hint: Walk the path forward and stop at the first stage that cannot account for the rows.
variants.explanation: Outcomes without exposure mean the join is measuring eligibility rather than treatment, so the estimate is held until the gap is explained.

variants.title: Trace one unit through the test
variants.context: One traceable experiment path runs from eligibility through a deterministic bucket, an exposure event, the outcome join, and finally the decision record. Assignment establishes intent; the exposure event proves the unit met the treatment.
variants.prompt: A second experiment must not overlap with the first. Put the stages in order for the unit that enters both surfaces.

items.text: Stable bucket: a distinct experiment ID and salt keep the two bucket assignments independent.
Decision record: interaction risk and the exclusion set are preserved beside both rollout actions.
Outcome join: shared outcomes are attributed under each experiment's own window and deduplication rule.
Eligibility: mutual-exclusion rules decide whether this unit may enter the second experiment at all.
Exposure log: each delivered experience is recorded under its own experiment and treatment version.

variants.hint: Two experiments share a user but must not share a bucket.
variants.explanation: Mutual exclusion and separate salts are what keep two concurrent experiments from silently becoming one confounded comparison.

variants.title: Budget the evidence
variants.context: Power depends on the baseline rate, the minimum detectable effect, allocation, and the number of independent units. Halving the target effect needs roughly four times the evidence, and a small treatment arm becomes the bottleneck.
variants.prompt: A checkout test is planned for a 1.0 percentage point minimum detectable effect and needs 60000 units in total. The team halves the target to 0.5 points with baseline rate, power, and allocation unchanged. Roughly how many units does the plan now need?
variants.hint: Sensitivity does not trade against sample size one for one.
variants.explanation: Halving the minimum detectable effect needs roughly four times as much evidence, so 60000 becomes about 240000 units.

mistakes.feedback: That doubles the sample, which is the linear guess rather than the roughly quadratic relationship.
That halves the sample, treating a smaller target effect as a cheaper measurement.

variants.title: Budget the evidence
variants.context: Power depends on the baseline rate, the minimum detectable effect, allocation, and the number of independent units. Halving the target effect needs roughly four times the evidence, and a small treatment arm becomes the bottleneck.
variants.prompt: A checkout conversion plan needs 34000 units per arm in a two-arm test. The surface sees 20000 visitors per day but only 8500 eligible units per day. How many days of collection does the plan require?
variants.hint: Count every arm, and count only the traffic that can actually enter.
variants.explanation: Two arms need 68000 units, and at 8500 eligible units per day the plan runs 8 days, because runtime is estimated from eligible traffic rather than total traffic.

mistakes.feedback: That sizes one arm only and forgets the control group needs the same evidence.
That divides by total site traffic instead of the eligible units that can enter the experiment.

variants.title: Budget the evidence
variants.context: Power depends on the baseline rate, the minimum detectable effect, allocation, and the number of independent units. Halving the target effect needs roughly four times the evidence, and a small treatment arm becomes the bottleneck.
variants.prompt: A risky candidate is limited to a 10 percent treatment allocation. The plan still requires 30000 exposed units in the treatment arm. How much total experiment traffic must flow through the test?
variants.hint: The small arm sets the pace for everything else.
variants.explanation: At a 10 percent allocation the treatment arm is the bottleneck, so reaching 30000 treated units requires about 300000 total units.

mistakes.feedback: That is the total a balanced 50/50 design would need, which is why the small allocation costs traffic.
That is the control side alone, which is what the other 90 percent of traffic receives.

variants.title: Diagnose the broken comparison
variants.context: Before lift is interpreted, the experiment itself has to be valid. Interference, outcome capture that depends on the variant, and mid-test definition changes all break the comparison rather than shrink it.
variants.prompt: In a two-sided marketplace, treated buyers are shown more aggressive recommendations, and the inventory they claim disappears from control buyers' results. Lift looks strong. What is the problem?
options: Treatment changes the inventory control sees, so the measured difference represents neither experience alone.
Control buyers are simply a weaker cohort, so the comparison needs covariate adjustment at analysis time.
The recommendation model is overfitting to treated buyers, so the fix is retraining on the full population.
optionFeedback: Correct: interference across units breaks exchangeability, so a cluster, marketplace, or switchback design is needed.
Randomization already balanced the cohorts; adjustment cannot undo an effect that traveled between the groups.
Model quality is a separate question, and retraining would not stop one buyer's treatment from depleting another's inventory.
variants.hint: Ask whether one unit's treatment can change another unit's experience.
variants.explanation: When units affect one another the assignment unit must move to the interference boundary, because a contaminated control no longer represents the control experience.

variants.title: Diagnose the broken comparison
variants.context: Before lift is interpreted, the experiment itself has to be valid. Interference, outcome capture that depends on the variant, and mid-test definition changes all break the comparison rather than shrink it.
variants.prompt: A new checkout flow logs its success event only after the confirmation page renders. Treatment users who hit an error never reach that page, and their sessions produce no outcome row at all. What does the analysis show?
options: A latency regression that will surface in the guardrails once p95 timings are added to the report.
An inflated treatment conversion rate, because failures are dropped from the treatment denominator.
An unbiased estimate with wider intervals, since the missing rows only reduce the treatment sample size.
optionFeedback: The errors may raise latency too, but the immediate defect is that failed sessions never enter the denominator.
Correct: outcome capture that depends on treatment success is missing not at random and biases the estimate upward.
Missing rows here are caused by the outcome itself, so this is bias rather than a simple loss of precision.
variants.hint: Ask whether a unit's chance of being logged depends on how the treatment went.
variants.explanation: Outcome capture that differs by variant is a validity failure, so exposure and outcome logging must be independent of whether the treatment succeeded.

variants.title: Diagnose the broken comparison
variants.context: Before lift is interpreted, the experiment itself has to be valid. Interference, outcome capture that depends on the variant, and mid-test definition changes all break the comparison rather than shrink it.
variants.prompt: On day five the analytics team redefines an active session from 15 minutes to 30 minutes for all traffic. The running test reads sessions per user as its primary metric. What should happen?
options: Treat the change as instrumentation drift, restart the measurement window under one definition, and note the split.
Keep collecting and compare only the post-change days for both arms once enough units have accumulated.
Apply the new definition retroactively to the earlier days so the whole window shares one session rule.
optionFeedback: Correct: a metric definition that changes mid-test makes the early and late windows non-comparable measurements.
That quietly abandons the planned window and stopping rule, leaving a shortened test nobody sized.
Recomputing history is only valid if the raw events support the new rule exactly, which is rarely verified in place.
variants.hint: Ask whether the same quantity was measured on day one and day nine.
variants.explanation: Metric definitions, event schemas, and attribution windows are frozen for the run, because a mid-test change measures two different quantities under one name.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: An experiment contract is assembled from parts with separate jobs. Each clause freezes one thing, each validity failure has its own name, and each design alternative exists for a specific reason a plain A/B test cannot handle.
variants.prompt: Match each clause of the experiment contract to what it freezes.

pairs.label: Experimental unit
pairs.detail: Who is assigned, chosen to match the boundary where interference can occur.

pairs.label: Treatment
pairs.detail: What changes, versioned across model, features, prompt, policy, and serving configuration.

pairs.label: Outcome contract
pairs.detail: What decides, naming one primary metric, a worthwhile effect, guardrails, and segments.

pairs.label: Stopping rule
pairs.detail: When it ends, fixing sample size or a valid sequential rule and the action for each result.

variants.hint: Each clause answers a different question that cannot be settled after the data arrives.
variants.explanation: The contract is a decision protocol, so freezing the unit, treatment, outcome, and stopping rule is what keeps the result interpretable.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: An experiment contract is assembled from parts with separate jobs. Each clause freezes one thing, each validity failure has its own name, and each design alternative exists for a specific reason a plain A/B test cannot handle.
variants.prompt: Match each validity failure to the symptom that reveals it.

pairs.label: Sample-ratio mismatch
pairs.detail: Observed group counts differ materially from the planned allocation.

pairs.label: Cross-variant exposure
pairs.detail: One unit receives both experiences inside the measurement window.

pairs.label: Missing not at random
pairs.detail: Outcome capture differs by variant or depends on whether the treatment succeeded.

pairs.label: Instrumentation drift
pairs.detail: Metric definitions, event schemas, or attribution windows change mid-test.

variants.hint: Each symptom is checked before lift is interpreted, not after.
variants.explanation: Named validity failures are detected from their own symptoms, because each one breaks the comparison in a way no analysis adjustment repairs.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: An experiment contract is assembled from parts with separate jobs. Each clause freezes one thing, each validity failure has its own name, and each design alternative exists for a specific reason a plain A/B test cannot handle.
variants.prompt: Match each situation to the design that replaces a plain A/B test.

pairs.label: Units affect one another
pairs.detail: Cluster, marketplace, or switchback designs that assign at the interference boundary.

pairs.label: Rare but unacceptable harm
pairs.detail: Pre-release safety evaluation, constrained canaries, expert review, and hard abort rules.

pairs.label: Outcomes arrive months later
pairs.detail: Validated leading indicators used carefully, plus preserved long-term holdouts.

variants.hint: Ask what property of the outcome makes an average over a short window misleading.
variants.explanation: A standard A/B test assumes independent units, tolerable worst cases, and outcomes inside the window, so each broken assumption has its own design.
